answer.generated: A deadlock can occur in a database system when multiple transactions simultaneously hold locks on different resources and attempt to acquire additional locks that are currently held by other transactions, leading to an impasse where each transaction waits indefinitely for the others to release their locks. This situation arises when two or more transactions are waiting for each other to unlock data, creating a circular wait condition. In the context of database transactions, shared (r_lock) locks allow multiple transactions to read the same data simultaneously without conflict, as more than one lock of this type can be active on one piece of data at one time. Conversely, exclusive (w_lock) locks are required before a transaction can write to a piece of data, ensuring that no other transaction can concurrently read or write to the same data until the lock is released, thus preventing conflicts during write operations. For example, if Transaction A acquires an r_lock on data X and then Transaction B attempts to acquire an r_lock on the same data X while holding an r_lock on another piece of data Y, and Transaction A subsequently tries to obtain an w_lock on data Y while holding an r_lock on data X, both transactions will be unable to proceed, resulting in a deadlock due to the circular wait condition.
